stories.headline: Update: Alberta Votes Monday on Starting Legal Process Toward Separation Referendum
stories.summary:
Voters in Alberta, home to the world's fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will decide on Oct. 19 whether the province should remain in Canada or begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. The vote is non-binding and does not itself decide whether Alberta leaves the country. Premier Danielle Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, has said support for starting the separation process, which stood at around 23% in a recent poll, is "still too high for my liking."

An Associated Press analysis traces how separatism moved from a fringe cause to a ballot question. Alberta has long feuded with Ottawa over oil and federal power, and Liberal prime ministers Pierre Trudeau and Justin Trudeau were deeply unpopular there over energy policy, including the national carbon tax and other climate measures. Separatist parties typically drew only 1% or 2% of the vote, according to former Premier Jason Kenney.

Kenney said the pandemic and the 2022 Freedom Convoy changed that, as activists "needed a new cause" and it "naturally morphed into separatism." Independence movement leader Jeff Rath cited federal vaccine rules barring unvaccinated Canadians from flying as his breaking point. Kenney said the movement has since professionalized, building organizations, raising money and drawing in experienced political operatives.

The vote comes as Prime Minister Mark Carney, who appeared at a Forever Canadian rally in Edmonton on Oct. 16, says the United States is trying to break Canada. The result will be watched as a gauge of separatist strength and of the strain between Alberta and the federal government.

stories.headline: No Kings Coalition Holds Thousands of Protests for Early-Voting 'Day of Action'
stories.summary:
The No Kings Coalition is staging thousands of events across the country on Saturday, Oct. 17, in what it calls a nationwide day of action timed to the start of early voting in many states. Previous nationwide protest days organized by the coalition were aimed at denouncing President Trump and his administration's policies.

This weekend the coalition is shifting strategy toward voter turnout ahead of the midterm elections. Organizers describe Saturday's events as a nonpartisan effort to get people to the polls, rather than a march focused on a single grievance.

The coalition's critics, including many Republicans, have characterized the movement as an anti-Trump operation despite the nonpartisan framing. Supporters say the events are about civic participation and opposing what they view as executive overreach. The turnout push comes as both parties intensify midterm campaigning, with Trump holding rallies in battleground states and Democrats leading in polls and fundraising.

stories.headline: Immigrant ICE Sought in Houston Reportedly Dead for Years After Agent Struck Worker with Vehicle
stories.summary:
The immigrant that federal agents were pursuing when an Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer struck a man with a vehicle in Houston has apparently been dead for almost a decade, according to an immigration advocacy group. The injured man, 48-year-old Miguel Parra Hernandez of Mexico, who is in the country without legal status, was driving to work Saturday morning when federal agents confronted him. He remains hospitalized with multiple leg fractures.

The Guardian reported that a federal officer slammed a vehicle into the construction worker and broke his leg, apparently believing him to be a man who died years ago in similar circumstances, according to the dead man's family. The family said the circumstances further call into question the account given by ICE.

ICE has defended its enforcement operations in general, and supporters of the administration argue that agents face dangerous situations and must act on available intelligence. Critics and immigration advocates say the incident points to flawed targeting and inadequate accountability. The case follows other disputes over ICE practices, including the agency's rejection of a GAO recommendation on automatic body-camera activation.

stories.headline: Final Trump Arch Plans Omit Previously Touted Military Complex
stories.summary:
Final site plans for President Trump's proposed 250-foot-tall triumphal arch do not mention the military features he previously said he would add to the project. The documentation was submitted by the Interior Department to the National Capital Planning Commission, according to reporting by The Hill and Bloomberg.

The president announced the structure in late September, with a site slated between Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial area. The omission of the military complex raises questions about whether those elements have been dropped, deferred or will be handled separately from the arch itself.

The planning commission review is the next step for the project. Supporters view the arch as a fitting national monument, while critics question its scale, cost and placement near Arlington National Cemetery.

stories.headline: Update: Katie Zacharia Ousted as White House Press Secretary After Five Days
stories.summary:
White House press secretary Katie Zacharia was pushed out on Friday after only five days in the job, according to two senior administration officials. A White House official said she was "transitioning out" of the role. She becomes the shortest-tenured press secretary in modern history, surpassing the record previously held by Anthony Scaramucci's brief stint as communications director.

Her exit followed a widely criticized first press briefing and questions about her credentials. She had described herself as a lawyer, but earlier this week it emerged that she did not pass the bar exam. President Trump told reporters he had said to her, "you don't have to do this if you don't want to," and "honestly, if I were you, I'd reconsider," adding that the news media had been harsh toward her. In a post on X on Friday night, Zacharia said it was an honor to work for the president.

The departure has revived questions about turmoil inside the West Wing. Reporting from several outlets describes infighting that spilled into public view this week, and Trump was pressed on the future of Chief of Staff Susie Wiles. Former acting chief of staff Mick Mulvaney said the administration "set her up to fail" by not preparing her adequately, and called Wiles's tenure "anybody's guess." Critics of the administration describe a chaotic communications operation weeks before the midterms, while supporters say the president was right to defend her against what he called unfair media treatment. No successor has been named.

stories.headline: Oregon Teacher Fought School Shooter Before Armed Father Killed Suspect, Police Say
stories.summary:
Police in Bend, Oregon, said a female teacher tackled a 16-year-old gunman who entered her classroom at Silver Rail Elementary and tried to wrestle the shotgun from him. She threw her phone and struggled with him on the floor, and was not injured. Police Chief Mike Krantz said her actions "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed."

The attack on Thursday killed three children and a teacher. Police identified two victims on Friday: five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert. The families of an eight-year-old and an 11-year-old did not want them named yet. Two others were wounded, a 54-year-old teacher who remains hospitalized and a seven-year-old student in serious but stable condition.

The suspect, identified as Griffin J John II, was a former special-education student at the school. He fired as many as 15 rounds and carried about 44 more rounds of ammunition. He was shot dead by a father who was driving past with two daughters at the school and ran in armed with a pistol. Family members identified him to media as 36-year-old carpenter Kaylub Giamanco. Police have not established a motive, are investigating how the suspect obtained the gun, and have executed a search warrant at his home.

The case has renewed debate over school safety. Gun-rights supporters point to the armed bystander as evidence that armed citizens can stop attacks, while gun-control advocates question whether gun-free-zone policies and access to firearms by minors contributed.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says California Officials Will 'Go to Jail' If They Count Ballots of Suspected Noncitizens
stories.summary:
President Trump on Saturday repeated a Justice Department warning that California election officials could face criminal charges if they tabulate mail-in ballots from more than 200,000 people the federal government has identified as potential noncitizens. "They will all go to jail for a long period of time!!!" he wrote. The statement escalates a dispute over the state's voter rolls less than three weeks before the November 3 midterms.

The DOJ sued California over claims it has not purged noncitizens from its rolls. In a letter sent Friday, senior department officials warned local officials that knowingly processing and counting ballots cast by noncitizens could expose them to criminal investigation and prosecution. The administration and its allies say the step is needed to enforce federal law and protect election integrity.

California officials and voting-rights advocates have pushed back, arguing the federal list is unreliable and that noncitizen voting is extremely rare. They fear the federal government is using the threat of prosecution to intimidate election workers, discourage participation or cast doubt on the results. Previous coverage noted a separate DOJ suit seeking to block the counting of about 20,000 ballots. The president's new remarks add a direct threat of jail time, and it remains unclear whether any charges will follow before votes are counted.

stories.headline: Three Men Sentenced to 158 Years Each for Murders of Australian and US Surfers in Mexico
stories.summary:
A Mexican judge sentenced three men to 158 years and nine months in prison each for murdering Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson and their American friend Carter Rhoad. The verdict was delivered last week, and the sentencing followed on Friday. The men were identified only as Jesus Gerardo, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus under Mexican legal rules.

The three surfers were killed in 2024 during an apparent botched robbery of their truck on a secluded beach in Baja California, about 36 hours after crossing from the US. Their bodies were dumped in a well with gunshot wounds to the head and were found a week later. Debra Robinson, the brothers' mother, told the court the killings had taken "the future we had imagined with them."

The alleged ringleader, Jesus Gerardo, known as "El Kekas," is among the convicted. His girlfriend was sentenced to 20 years in a separate trial last November after admitting involvement in the robbery. The case shocked Australia and unsettled tourists and residents in Ensenada, a popular surf destination usually seen as safe, and prompted local surfers to demand better security in a state where tourism is a key part of the economy.

stories.headline: Trump Waives New Russia Sanctions in 'National Interests,' Drawing Bipartisan Criticism
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump signed an executive order late Friday waiving sanctions, restrictions and duties on Russia that were due to take effect under a sweeping sanctions package he signed into law last month. The legislation, dedicated posthumously to the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, was meant to pressure the Kremlin and included hefty tariffs on large-scale buyers of Russian energy. Trump told Congress the pause was in the national interest.

Reporting indicates the measures complicated the administration's effort to lower diesel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. The waiver follows a surprise deal last week allowing Russia to sell diesel internationally, a move Republicans have condemned as loudly as Democrats. Sen. Thom Tillis, a North Carolina Republican, called the decision "beyond irresponsible," and several other GOP lawmakers also criticized it.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said things were "difficult" without the support of Graham, and reported that Russia had targeted Ukraine's energy sector with more than 320 drones, missiles and munitions. Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto told the BBC the United States risks prolonging Russia's full-scale invasion rather than helping end it.

The administration has framed the step as a way to ease energy prices for American consumers. Critics in both parties argue it relaxes pressure on Moscow while the war continues. Congress could respond in the coming days as lawmakers weigh whether to challenge the waiver.

stories.headline: Fact Check: Trump's Midterm Rally Claims on Immigration Costs and Leakers
stories.summary:
As President Trump campaigns in battleground states ahead of the midterms, PBS NewsHour's Liz Landers fact-checked several claims from his recent rallies. At an Ohio rally, Trump said Somali immigrants drive up taxes, health care, insurance and childcare costs and "cheat on everything."

Landers noted that the Congressional Budget Office projects the immigration surge that began in 2024 will add $1.2 trillion to federal revenue over ten years, with the annual increase reaching $164 billion by 2034. Undocumented immigrants are not eligible for Medicaid, and lawfully present immigrants generally face a five-year wait. KFF has found immigrants are not more likely than U.S.-born citizens to report using government assistance for food, housing or health care.

At an Arizona rally, Trump said "leakers should be shot," apparently referring to recent leaks about U.S. strikes on Iran. Landers noted most leaks are prosecuted under the Espionage Act of 1917, which carries severe penalties but is not typically applied as a death-penalty statute for leaking.

Trump's supporters view his rally rhetoric as a forceful articulation of concerns about immigration and national security, and Republicans see the rallies as key to energizing the base. Critics, including many Democrats, say the claims are inaccurate and inflammatory. Eleven outlets across the political spectrum covered the remarks and the fact-checking.

stories.headline: Community Leaders Link Foiled Hindu Temple Attack in Illinois to Surge in Online Hate
stories.summary:
Authorities arrested 19-year-old Alexandros Paporakis on Wednesday in connection with a thwarted mass shooting at the Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple in Aurora, Illinois. Officials said he drove to the temple Sunday afternoon with a rifle and body armor and waited in the parking lot for several minutes before leaving after his weapon jammed. Thousands were inside observing the first day of Navaratri.

Paporakis was arrested near his home in Palatine after a co-worker at a Taco Bell alerted authorities to his stated plan to "kill Indian people." Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, who was inside the temple with his parents, said the community was shaken. At a Friday news conference in Chicago, he and other leaders called for the attempted attack to be investigated as a hate crime.

Community advocates said anti-Hindu and anti-Indian rhetoric has grown online. Pushpita Prasad of the Coalition of Hindus of North America warned that "sooner or later, all that online hate is going to migrate to the real world." Recent incidents include bricks thrown at a temple in Richmond Heights, Ohio, on Oct. 3, and a June 2025 shooting at a temple in Spanish Fork, Utah.

Leaders are calling for an organized community response to prevent hate and extremism targeting all communities.

stories.headline: Tesla Unveils Roadster With Thrusters That Let It Hover and Turn in Mid-Air
stories.summary:
Tesla unveiled a new version of its Roadster electric sports car in Texas, equipped with thrusters that appear to allow it to hover and turn in mid-air. CEO Elon Musk presented the vehicle at a facility owned by his SpaceX company, which helped develop the model.

"You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk told the audience, saying a live crowd was needed to prove the demonstration "is not AI." The car was shown driving up and off a steep ramp, spinning in the air and landing using air jets.

The BBC's technology editor Zoe Kleinman said there are several reasons a flying car is unlikely to appear on public roads anytime soon. The unveiling was covered by ABC News, BBC News and CBS News.

stories.headline: Update: Houthis Strike Aden Airport and Saudi Aramco Complex as Iran War Widens
stories.summary:
Yemen's Houthi rebels struck the main airport in the interim capital of Aden on Friday, while missiles and drones fired toward Saudi Arabia were intercepted, Bloomberg reported. The attack followed ballistic missile strikes on al-Maashiq Palace, after which Yemen's information minister said the prime minister and other ministers were unhurt. The Saudi energy ministry said a Houthi attack caused a "limited fire" at Aramco's headquarters complex in Dhahran.

The fighting is also reaching beyond Yemen's borders. A dozen people were killed Saturday in what Saudi aviation authorities called a "brutal" attack at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. The Houthi missile strikes also threaten key supply routes on Yemen's Red Sea coast, intensifying pressure on government forces. BBC security correspondent Frank Gardner said the Iran-backed group's precision strikes and guerrilla tactics have made it hard for Saudi forces to gain the upper hand.

The escalation is tied to the wider war with Iran. Data from a monitoring agency shows attacks around the Strait of Hormuz at a record high, with two more vessels reporting attacks Friday, and all 21 sailors on the Singapore-flagged GFS Pride were evacuated safely after it was struck by a projectile. Adm. Brad Cooper, the US Central Command commander, said Friday that the US naval blockade has cost Iran $25 billion in crude oil revenue. Experts say US military assistance and shuttle tankers and pipelines bypassing Hormuz have helped Gulf exports rebound. Analysts expect continued strikes on Saudi infrastructure, and no sign of de-escalation has emerged.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Denies Restricting Ukraine's Starlink Access as Reuters Cites White House Order
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump denied that he or Elon Musk limited Ukraine's access to Starshield, the military-grade counterpart to Starlink. "It wasn't me and I don't think it was Elon," he said, adding that he was "not sure" the network "ever came down." Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said earlier that normal speeds had not been restored.

Reuters reported Thursday, citing two unnamed US officials and a Western official, that the order came from inside the White House. Musk suggested the US government manages Starshield and that the Pentagon could have been responsible. On Tuesday night, speeds were reportedly capped at 100 mph, cutting off connectivity to faster weapons, and Ukraine was hit by several deadly strikes that left about 600,000 people without power.

The dispute follows tension over a US-Russia diesel deal and Zelensky's resumption of strikes on Russian refineries, which Trump criticized. Washington had earlier warned it could withhold intelligence if the strikes continued. Trump said he has a good relationship with Zelensky, though he had earlier called him "more difficult to deal with" than Vladimir Putin. Zelensky told EU leaders on Friday, "If I don't stand up to this... who else will?" while French President Emmanuel Macron pledged that EU states would not abandon Ukraine. A bipartisan group of senators has demanded an investigation into the disruption, which they said degraded Ukraine's defensive operations.

stories.headline: Update: Midterm Fight Intensifies as Democrats Lead Polls and Fundraising, Justice Department Warns California Officials
stories.summary:
Less than three weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms, a national Times/Siena poll showed Democrats leading the congressional ballot by nearly nine percentage points. Democratic Senate candidates in more than a dozen competitive races raised a combined $253 million from July through September, more than four times the $56 million raised by Republicans in those races. Alaska is emerging as a pivotal contest, where Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola clashed in a debate over fuel costs tied to the war with Iran and allegations about Peltola's treatment of staff.

The Justice Department escalated its fight with California, warning in a letter that local officials who knowingly tabulate ballots cast by noncitizens could face criminal investigation and prosecution. Voting rights advocates fear the administration could use federal power to cast doubt on the election's results. Administration supporters say the actions are needed to enforce voter-roll requirements and keep noncitizens from voting.

Republicans face a difficult environment. Trump's approval stands near 37 percent, according to Silver Bulletin, and some conservatives are blaming Senate Majority Leader John Thune for failing to pass the SAVE America Act. Democrats are working to tie GOP opponents to Trump's economic policies and the Iran war. The House majority is thin, with Republicans holding 218 seats, and Cook rates 21 districts as toss-ups. Suspicious letters have also been sent to election offices and congressional offices, which federal investigators are examining.

stories.headline: Update: More Lawmakers Report Suspicious Mailings as Federal Investigators Probe Letters
stories.summary:
Several lawmakers said Friday that their offices across the country had received suspicious mailings. The reports follow earlier ones this week of letters containing unknown substances sent to US election offices. Among those affected are Sens. Amy Klobuchar, Tina Smith, Mike Rounds, Pete Ricketts and Ted Cruz, along with more than 15 House members.

Federal investigators said they are looking into the letters containing unknown substances mailed to state election officials and congressional offices. The incidents span both parties and several states. The substances have not been publicly identified in the reports provided.

The mailings come weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm elections, adding security concerns for election administrators already dealing with legal disputes and heightened tension over ballot counting. Further details on the investigation's findings are expected.
